pr.title: mir_transform: implement `#[rustc_force_inline]`
pr.description:
Adds `#[rustc_force_inline]` which is similar to always inlining but reports an error if the inlining was not possible.

- `#[rustc_force_inline]` can only be applied to free functions to guarantee that the MIR inliner will be able to resolve calls.
- `rustc_mir_transform::inline::Inline` is refactored into two passes (`Inline` and `ForceInline`), sharing the vast majority of the implementation.
  - `rustc_mir_transform::inline::ForceInline` can't be disabled so annotated items are always inlined.
  - `rustc_mir_transform::inline::ForceInline` runs regardless of optimisation level.
- `#[rustc_force_inline]` won't inline unless target features match, as with normal inlining.
- MIR validation will ICE if a `#[rustc_force_inline]` isn't inlined, to guarantee that it will never be codegened independently. As a further guarantee, monomorphisation collection will always decide that `#[rustc_force_inline]` functions cannot be codegened locally.
- Like other intrinsics, `#[rustc_force_inline]` annotated functions cannot be cast to function pointers.
- As with other rustc attrs, this cannot be used by users, just within the compiler and standard library.
- This is only implemented within rustc, so should avoid any limitations of LLVM's inlining.

It is intended that this attribute be used with intrinsics that must be inlined for security reasons. For example, pointer authentication intrinsics would allow Rust users to make use of pointer authentication instructions, but if these intrinsic functions were in the binary then they could be used as gadgets with ROP attacks, defeating the point of introducing them. We don't have any intrinsics like this today, but I expect to upstream some once a force inlining mechanism such as this is available.

cc rust-lang/rust#131687 rust-lang/rfcs#3711 - this approach should resolve the concerns from these previous attempts

processing.reason: The PR adds the compiler-internal `#[rustc_force_inline]` feature. The historical baseline difference is pass behavior: a direct call may remain a `TerminatorKind::Call` instead of being inlined, and the corrected behavior splices the callee body (or rejects inlining with an error). Inlining a direct call is semantics-preserving for defined executions: both the un-inlined call and the spliced body execute the same callee code and produce the same value. The PR's actual guarantees are compile-time/MIR/codegen-level: MIR-dump scope `(inlined callee_forced)`, diagnostics for non-inlinable callees, function-pointer-cast rejection, and monomorphization root restrictions. Its tests are MIR-opt diffs and UI `build-fail` tests, not value regressions. Target-feature/instruction-set/inline-asm mismatches are rejected at compile time, and MC/DC coverage likewise, so they cannot produce two different defined runtime values. Constructing a pair that returns different values would require inventing an observable “was inlined” flag, which is not a historical semantic transformation and is forbidden by the task. Hence no valid source-grounded counterexample pair exists.

analysis.originalLogic: The pre-PR inliner is a single `Inline` MIR pass with one `Inliner` implementation. It decides whether to splice a direct call using codegen-attribute checks, MIR-availability checks, cost thresholds, and `inline_limit_for_block`, and it can be disabled or overridden like an ordinary optimization pass. There is no `ForceInline` pass and no `InlineAttr::Force` variant.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect baseline for this feature is the ordinary inliner outcome: a direct call to a `#[rustc_force_inline]` free function may remain as a `TerminatorKind::Call` in optimized MIR because normal policy, cost limits, opt level, or pass overrides skipped inlining, or the callee may be treated as an ordinary inlining candidate without enforcing the forced-inlining invariants. The corrected transformation must splice the callee body at every resolvable direct call, and must reject inlining when the callee cannot legally be moved, rather than silently leaving the call.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust MIR function bodies containing direct calls to free functions annotated `#[rustc_force_inline]`, at `-Copt-level=0` as well as optimized levels. Callers include ordinary free functions, closure bodies, async/coroutine bodies, and shims. Callees may be local or cross-crate, empty, contain inline asm, have `#[target_feature]`/`#[instruction_set]`, or be used as `FnOnce` arguments. The attribute is compiler-internal and gated by `#![feature(rustc_attrs)]`.
analysis.summary: `ForceInline` is a non-overridable MIR pass that must inline every direct call to a `#[rustc_force_inline]` free function regardless of optimization level, while `Inline` keeps normal cost-based behavior and `Validator` enforces the postcondition that no optimized MIR still calls a force-inline function.
analysis.trigger: A basic-block terminator is a direct call whose callee is an `InstanceKind::Item` and whose `tcx.codegen_fn_attrs(def_id).inline` is `InlineAttr::Force { .. }`. `ForceInline` runs immediately before the normal `Inline` pass and also in shim construction.
preconditions: The callee is a free function annotated with `#[rustc_force_inline]`; the attribute cannot be applied to a closure, coroutine, async/gen function, or non-function item.
The attribute is enabled only under `#![feature(rustc_attrs)]` and is intended for compiler/std-library use.
The callee must not be `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]`, `#[cold]`, C-variadic, or an intrinsic, and its body must not contain tail calls.
The callee MIR must be available and resolvable; the caller must be a function/closure body.
Target features must match exactly and instruction sets must be compatible; a callee containing inline asm cannot be moved across an incompatible instruction set.
`ForceInline` must remain enabled at all optimization levels and must not be disabled by `-Zenable-mir-passes`.
After optimized MIR is produced, no remaining direct call may target an `InlineAttr::Force` function; monomorphization must not root or codegen such a function independently.
pitfalls: Do not model `#[rustc_force_inline]` as merely `#[inline(always)]`: the PR explicitly makes `ForceInline` non-overridable, runs it regardless of opt level, and turns failure to inline into an error.

`ForceInline` and normal `Inline` share implementation but use different policies: `ForceInline` ignores normal cost/threshold limits and reports failures, while `Inline` still applies heuristic limits.

Coverage instrumentation had a known interaction: the old `Inline` pass bailed out under MC/DC coverage, so forced inlining must explicitly reject `instrument_coverage_mcdc()` rather than bypassing the marker.
Inlining across incompatible instruction sets is unsafe when the callee contains inline asm; the error reason is `cannot move inline-asm across instruction sets`.

`#[target_feature]` is not prohibited with `#[rustc_force_inline]` the way it is with `#[inline(always)]`; instead the MIR inliner must verify matching target-feature names and fail forced inlining if they differ.
Forcing inlining does not make function-pointer casts legal: casting a force-inline function to a fn pointer must be rejected so it cannot be codegened independently.
Monomorphization must not collect force-inline functions as roots or local copies; otherwise they can be codegened despite never being called after inlining.

The validator check is a postcondition, not a substitute for `ForceInline`: it must only fire for `TerminatorKind::Call`/`TailCall` in `MirPhase::Runtime(RuntimePhase::Optimized)` whose `FnDef` callee has `InlineAttr::Force`.
Async/closure callers require inlining inside the generated coroutine/closure body; the outer async function body itself may only construct the coroutine and legitimately show no inlined call.
analysis.testStrategy: Use MIR-opt tests with `-Copt-level=0 --crate-type=lib` and `EMIT_MIR_FOR_EACH_PANIC_STRATEGY`, checking the `ForceInline` before/after diff for `scope 1 (inlined callee_forced)` and removal of the call block. Cover ordinary free-fn caller, async caller, closure body caller, and dead-code caller (`-Clink-dead-code`). Add UI tests for invalid attribute placement, async/gen rejection, `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]`/cold/C-variadic early rejection, cross-crate forced inlining, function-pointer casts, instruction-set/inline-asm failure (`thumbv4t-none-eabi`), and a `build-pass` shim test that passes a force-inline fn to `FnOnce`. Use the expected diagnostic text to assert failure reasons rather than expecting silent non-inlining.

`rustc_mir_transform::inline::ForceInline` can't be disabled so annotated items are always inlined.
MIR validation will ICE if a `#[rustc_force_inline]` isn't inlined, to guarantee that it will never be codegened independently.
As a further guarantee, monomorphisation collection will always decide that `#[rustc_force_inline]` functions cannot be codegened locally.
Like other intrinsics, `#[rustc_force_inline]` annotated functions cannot be cast to function pointers.
`#[rustc_force_inline]` won't inline unless target features match, as with normal inlining.
